Chapter 1
Network Fundamentals

Personalised study document built from Todd Lammle, CCNA Certification Study Guide, Volume 2 (Exam 200-301, 2020), book pages 1-28. Section numbers (1.1, 1.2 ...) match the rows in your Notion tracker CCNA Knowledge Tracker.
| Item | Details |
| Book pages | 1-28 (review questions pp. 26-27, answers in the Appendix, p. 788) |
| Tracker rows | Chapter 1 and sections 1.1 to 1.5 (16 rows, Seq 1-16). All start as Not assessed. |

| Suggested time | One session of about 2 hours (this is a suggestion, not a measured need): pre-check 10 min, reading 1.1-1.3 about 40 min, reading 1.4-1.5 about 30 min, labs 30 min, review questions and tracker 10 min. |
| Exam versions | Written for you to study v1.1 (retires 2 Feb 2027) and see what changes in v2.0 (from 3 Feb 2027). Tags below show which applies. |
| Status of your knowledge | Not assessed. Nothing here assumes you know or do not know a topic. Do the pre-check first. |
How to read the tags
| Tag | Meaning |
| BOOK | Content taken from the Lammle chapter (book page given where useful). |
| UPDATED | The book is out of date or unclear here. The note says what changed and why. Nothing was silently replaced. |
| ADDED | Extra material that is not in this chapter but matters for the exam or real work. |
| CHECK | I could not verify this on real equipment or in an official source in this session. Check it in your lab. |
WHAT THE BOOK SAYS

Learning objectives (from the book): explain the role and function of network components (routers, L2 and L3 switches, next-generation firewalls and IPS); describe network topology architectures (2-tier, 3-tier, spine-leaf, WAN, SOHO); compare physical interface and cabling types (single-mode fibre, multimode fibre, copper, shared media and point-to-point, PoE).
Where this chapter fits in the exam
| Section | v1.1 objective | v2.0 outline (Cisco PDF) | Priority |
| 1.1 Network components | 1.1 Role of routers and L2/L3 switches | No separate objective in the v2.0 outline I read. Treat as foundation. | High (needed for everything later) |
| 1.2 NGFW and IPS | 1.1 NGFW and IPS | Not listed in the v2.0 outline I read. | Medium |
| 1.3 Topology architectures | 1.2 2-tier, 3-tier, spine-leaf, WAN, SOHO, on-premises and cloud | Not listed in the v2.0 outline I read. | Medium |

| 1.4 Physical interfaces and cables | 1.3 Interface and cable types; 1.4 Interface and cable issues | 1.1 Diagnose interface and cable (copper and fibre) issues: errors, duplex, speed, distance, signal levels, pin out, cable types | High |
| 1.5 Ethernet cabling and PoE | 1.3 Cabling; 1.1 PoE | 1.1 (cable types, pin out); 2.2 (PoE on edge-host switch ports) | High |
Cisco says its topic list is a guide and related topics may still appear, so a topic missing from the v2.0 outline is not a promise that it will not be tested.

sections.title: Step 0: Pre-check (do this before you read)

content.text: Answer from memory with no looking up. Write your answer and a confidence tag for each: (K) I know it, (U) unsure, (G) guessing. Wrong answers are useful. They tell us where to spend time. The answer key is at the end of this document (Answer Key A).
- Name the three layers of the Cisco hierarchical model. Give one job for each layer.
- A hub, a switch and a router: for each one, how many collision domains and how many broadcast domains does it create by default?
- Which cable type would you normally use to connect a switch to a switch? Which pins are crossed?
- What is the difference between single-mode and multimode fibre? Which one goes farther?
- What does PoE do, and which IEEE standard is called PoE+?

After answering, mark the section rows below in the tracker only if your answers give real evidence. One question is thin evidence. Use Partially understand or Need to learn honestly, and leave rows you did not test as Not assessed.
BOOK An internetwork is what you get when you connect two or more networks with a router and give them a logical addressing scheme such as IPv4 or IPv6.
Three devices, three jobs
| Device | OSI layer | Looks at | Collision domains | Broadcast domains |
| Hub | 1 (Physical) | Nothing. It repeats bits to every port. | One for the whole hub | One |
| Switch (Layer 2) | 2 (Data Link) | Destination MAC address in the frame | One per port | One (all ports, by default) |
| Router | 3 (Network) | Destination IP address in the packet | One per interface | One per interface (it splits them) |

Simple words: a collision domain is the group of devices that can interfere with each other when they send at the same time. A broadcast domain is the group of devices that all receive a message sent "to everyone". Switches fix the first problem. Only routers (or VLANs, later) fix the second.
EXAM CRITICAL

Hubs: one collision domain AND one broadcast domain. Switches: one collision domain per port, still one broadcast domain. Routers: split broadcast domains and do not forward broadcasts by default. You must be able to count domains on a diagram.
Why routers are used (book p. 5)
- They do not forward broadcasts by default, so a broadcast storm stays in its own network.
- They can filter traffic using Layer 3 information such as an IP address (for example with an access list, Chapter 10).
- They connect to WAN services. The book mentions a serial interface using a V.35 physical interface on Cisco routers.
What a Layer 2 switch really does (book pp. 5-6)

A switch is "hardware-based bridging". It uses a special chip called an ASIC so it can switch frames at very high speed with very low latency (the time from a frame entering a port to leaving a port).

The book calls the switch's memory a filter table. Cisco's everyday name is the MAC address table. Both mean the same thing: a list of which MAC address lives on which port. The switch builds it by watching source addresses. It makes decisions using destination addresses.
Command breakdown: the MAC address table
Illustrative output (your MAC addresses will differ)
Switch# show mac address-table
Mac Address Table
Vlan Mac Address Type Ports
- show mac address-table is a Privileged EXEC command. It shows what the switch has learned.
- Vlan: which VLAN the address was learned in (VLAN 1 is the default).
- Type DYNAMIC: learned automatically. STATIC means someone typed it in.
- Ports: where to send frames for that MAC address.
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE
The command was show mac-address-table on older IOS versions. Current IOS uses show mac address-table. CHECK If one form is rejected on your simulator, try the other.
The six steps of switch forwarding
- A frame arrives on a port.
- The switch learns: it records the frame's source MAC address and the port it arrived on.
- The switch looks up the destination MAC address in its table.
- Known, on a different port: it forwards the frame out of that one port only.
- Known, on the same port it arrived on: it filters (drops) the frame. Nobody else needs it. The book calls this transparent bridging.
- Unknown destination, or a broadcast: it floods the frame out of every port except the one it came in on.
MEMORY TIP
Learn by SOURCE, forward by DESTINATION. Unknown means flood.
Things that make a LAN slow (book p. 4)
- Too many hosts in one collision or broadcast domain
- Broadcast storms
- Too much multicast traffic
- Low bandwidth
- Adding hubs for connectivity
- Lots of ARP broadcasts
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)

Layer 3 switch. The book lists L2 and L3 switches in the objectives but only explains L2 here. A Layer 3 switch is a switch that can also route between VLANs and subnets, using interfaces called SVIs (switch virtual interfaces). It still switches at Layer 2 inside a VLAN. You will configure this in Chapter 8. ADDED
Also in the v1.1 objective but taught later in the book: access points, controllers, endpoints and servers (Chapters 18-20).
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

Hubs are obsolete. You will not find them in modern networks. They stay in the exam as a way to teach collision domains. The book also says a switch with a hub attached to one port makes that hub's hosts share one collision domain. That is still true and is a common exam picture.
Quick check 1.1
Q1. A switch receives a frame whose destination MAC address is not in its MAC address table. What does it do?
A. Drops it
B. Sends it back out of the port it arrived on
C. Floods it out of all other ports
D. Sends it to the router
Answer: C - unknown unicast frames are flooded out of every port except the incoming one.
Q2. Eight PCs connect to one switch (one PC per port), and the switch connects to one router interface. How many broadcast domains exist?
Answer: One - a switch does not split broadcast domains. The router interface is in the same one.
Q3. Name the two ways a router helps reduce traffic problems on a LAN.
Answer: It does not forward broadcasts by default, and it can filter by Layer 3 information. - these are the two advantages the book gives.

BOOK Networks need security as they grow. A traditional firewall allows or blocks traffic using rules about addresses and ports and by remembering connections (stateful inspection). A Next-Generation Firewall (NGFW) goes much deeper: it reassembles packets and inspects them "up to and through Layer 7", so it can understand the application and not just the port.
What an NGFW must do (book p. 8)
| Capability | Plain meaning |
| Router and switch compatible (L2/L3) | Can sit in the network as a routed or switched device |
| Packet filtering with IPS and malware inspection | Blocks known attacks and bad files |
| NAT | Translates private addresses (Chapter 11) |
| Stateful inspection | Remembers connections and allows return traffic |
| VPN | Builds encrypted tunnels (Chapter 15) |
| URL and application filtering | Allows or blocks by website category or app, e.g. block a game but allow email |
| QoS | Prioritises important traffic (Chapter 16) |
| Third-party integration, REST API support | Other tools can read it and control it automatically |
IPS in one minute

BOOK An Intrusion Prevention System (IPS) looks for attacks on known vulnerabilities and acts on them. NGFWs also offer Application Visibility and Control (AVC). Some can decrypt SSL/TLS traffic to inspect it, but that needs special hardware to stay fast and costs more.
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)

IDS versus IPS. ADDED An IDS (Intrusion Detection System) watches a copy of the traffic and only raises an alert. An IPS sits in the path of the traffic and can block the attack itself. The "P" means Prevention. The risk of an IPS is a false positive that blocks good traffic.
Where the firewall sits

The book's Figure 1.5 shows the usual order: Internet  Firewall  Router  Switches  hosts (PCs, printer, server, IP phone, access point). The firewall is the guard between the outside world and your inside network.
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

Names have changed. UPDATED The book calls Cisco's NGFW "Firepower" and says Firepower Threat Defense (FTD) is replacing the ASA. Cisco's current documentation calls the product Cisco Secure Firewall Threat Defense (formerly Firepower Threat Defense), and newer pages shorten it to Firewall Threat Defense. Cisco's rebranding guide says older hardware platforms still show Firepower branding in places, so you will see both names.

The ASA has not disappeared. Cisco's current reimage guide still lists ASA software versions (for example ASA 9.20 for the Firepower 2100 series). Think of it this way: new deployments use Threat Defense, but existing ASAs are still around and supported on some models.
Sourcefire: the book says Cisco acquired Sourcefire in 2013 and the technology became Firepower. That matches Cisco's history of the product line.
EXAM CRITICAL
For the exam: know what an NGFW adds over a plain stateful firewall (Layer 7 inspection, AVC, IPS, URL filtering, TLS decryption) and be able to say what an IPS does. Product names are not the point.
Quick check 1.2
Q4. Which feature lets an NGFW allow a company app but block a game running on the same port?
A. NAT
B. Application Visibility and Control
C. VLAN trunking
D. Port security
Answer: B - AVC identifies the application, not only the port number.
Q5. In one sentence, what is the difference between an IDS and an IPS?
Answer: An IDS only alerts; an IPS sits in the traffic path and can block. - that is the whole idea behind "detection" versus "prevention".
BOOK Hierarchy makes networks easier to design, predict and fix. It tells you which job belongs where. For example, you use access lists at some layers and avoid them at others.
1.3.1 The Cisco Three-Layer Hierarchical Model (3-Tier), book p. 10
The three layers are logical, not physical. Three layers does not mean three boxes. One device can do two jobs, and one layer can have many devices.
| Layer | Main job | Do | Do not |

| Core (backbone) | Move huge amounts of traffic reliably and fast | High reliability (redundant fast links)Low latencyRouting protocols with fast convergence | Slow traffic down: no access lists, no inter-VLAN routing, no packet filteringSupport workgroup accessExpand the core by adding routers (upgrade instead) |

| Distribution (workgroup or aggregation) | The meeting point between access and core. Routing, filtering, WAN access, policy. | Routing and inter-VLAN routingAccess lists, packet filtering, queuingSecurity and network policy, address translation, firewallsRedistribute between routing protocolsDefine broadcast and multicast domains | Do things that belong only to the core or access layers |

| Access (desktop) | Connect users and devices to the network | Separate collision domains (microsegmentation with switches)Workgroup connectivity to distributionDevice connectivity, resiliency and security servicesVoice/video capabilities and QoS marking | Make big routing decisions |
MEMORY TIP
Core = SPEED. Distribution = POLICY. Access = CONNECT.
WHY THIS MATTERS
A failure in the core can affect every user. That is why the core is built with redundancy and kept simple.
1.3.2 Collapsed Core (2-Tier), book p. 13

BOOK In a collapsed core design the core and distribution layers run on the same switches. It is cheaper and still works well for a campus that will not grow much. The access switches plug into the collapsed core. Other names: 2-tier, and the middle layer is also called aggregation.
1.3.3 Spine-Leaf, book p. 14

BOOK Used in data centres. Each rack has a top-of-rack (ToR) switch called a leaf. Servers connect to the leaf switches (often two leaves for redundancy). Every leaf connects to every spine. Spines connect only to leaves, never to servers. Cisco Nexus switches are the example in the book.
- Every leaf is the same distance from every other leaf: one spine hop, so latency is predictable.
- You do not need a huge number of cross-links between switches.
- Leaves connect to servers, firewalls, load balancers or a router leaving the data centre.
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)

Why data centres like it. ADDED Most data centre traffic goes server-to-server (east-west), not out to the internet (north-south). In a 3-tier tree that traffic climbs up and down layers. Spine-leaf gives every pair of leaves the same short path, and you add capacity by adding spines or leaves.
1.3.4 WAN, book p. 15

BOOK The main difference between a LAN and a WAN is usually ownership: you generally own a LAN, and you generally lease a WAN from a service provider. A WAN connects sites that are far apart, uses carriers (telcos, cable, satellite), and traditionally uses serial connections.
Why WANs exist (book): branch offices must share data, organisations share information across distance, and travelling staff need access to corporate resources.
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)

Modern WANs. ADDED CHECK The book only discusses classic leased-line terms. Today you will also hear about MPLS, Metro Ethernet, internet VPNs and SD-WAN. This is general knowledge and I did not verify it against a source in this session. Learn the idea (a provider or the internet carries traffic between your sites) and treat the details as later study.
1.3.5 Defining WAN Terms, book pp. 16-17
| Term | Meaning (from the book) |
| CPE (customer premises equipment) | Equipment owned by the subscriber, on the subscriber's site |
| CSU/DSU | Connects a DTE (your router) to a digital circuit such as T1/T3. Remember: it provides clocking to the router. Connects to the router by serial cable. |
| Demarc (demarcation point) | The exact point where the provider's responsibility ends and the CPE begins. Usually a box in a telecom closet. You cable from it to your CPE (the "extended demarc"). |
| Local loop | Connects the demarc to the nearest provider switching office |
| Central office (CO) | Connects your network to the provider's switching network. Also called a point of presence (POP). |
| Toll network | The trunk lines inside the provider's network |
| Optical fibre converter | Converts optical signals to electrical and back where fibre ends |
MEMORY TIP
Order from your building to the provider: CPE  demarc  local loop  CO  toll network.
1.3.6 WAN Connection Bandwidth, book p. 17
| Name | Made of | Speed |
| DS0 | One channel (E0 in Europe, J0 in Japan) | 64 Kbps |
| E1 | 30 x DS0 (European T1) | 2.048 Mbps |
| OC-3 | 3 x DS3 = 2,016 DS0 (fibre) | 155.52 Mbps |
I checked the multiplication in the book's table: 28 x 24 = 672, 672 x 3 = 2,016, 2,016 x 4 = 8,064 and 8,064 x 4 = 32,256. All consistent.
SOHO and on-premises versus cloud

BOOK SOHO means small office / home office: a small network for one user or a few users, usually one router, one or two switches and a firewall, connecting them to the internet and to resources like printers and servers (book Exam Essentials).
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)

On-premises and cloud. ADDED CHECK The v1.1 objective 1.2 lists "on-premises and cloud", but I did not find it in this chapter. In plain words: on-premises means you own and run the equipment in your own building. Cloud means you rent computing, storage or networking from a provider over the internet. Know the three service models (IaaS, PaaS, SaaS) and the deployment types (public, private, hybrid). I wrote this from general knowledge and have not checked Cisco's exact wording.
Quick check 1.3
Q6. Which layer of the 3-tier model should avoid access lists and packet filtering, and why?
A. Access
B. Distribution
C. Core
D. All of them
Answer: C - the core should switch traffic as fast as possible; policy belongs in the distribution layer.
Q7. In a spine-leaf design, what do spine switches connect to?
A. Servers
B. Leaf switches only
C. Other spine switches and servers
D. Firewalls only
Answer: B - spines connect only to leaves; every leaf connects to every spine.
Q8. Which WAN device provides clocking to a router's serial interface?
Answer: The CSU/DSU - the book says clocking is the most important thing to remember about it.
Q9. Where does the provider's responsibility end?
Answer: At the demarc (demarcation point) - after that, the cabling and equipment are the customer's.

BOOK Ethernet was first built by DIX (Digital, Intel, Xerox) at 10 Mbps on coax. The IEEE turned it into 802.3, then added 802.3u (Fast Ethernet), 802.3ab (Gigabit on category 5 copper), 802.3ae (10 Gbps over fibre) and later 100 Gbps (802.3ba). The EIA/TIA sets the physical-layer rules, including the RJ45 connector (the book notes it is really an 8-pin modular connector) on UTP cable.
Three words you must know
| Word | Meaning |
| Attenuation | Signal getting weaker as it travels along the cable. Measured in decibels (dB). Better cable = lower attenuation. |
| Crosstalk | Unwanted signal leaking between wire pairs in the same cable. More twists per foot = less crosstalk. |
| Category (Cat) | A quality rating for copper cable. A higher category has less crosstalk and attenuation. |
Ethernet standards table (book pp. 18-19)
| Name | IEEE | Speed | Medium | Max distance (book) |
| 10Base-T | 802.3 | 10 Mbps | Cat3 UTP | 100 m |
| 100Base-TX | 802.3u | 100 Mbps | Cat5/5e/6 UTP, 2 pairs | 100 m |
| 100Base-FX | 802.3u | 100 Mbps | 62.5/125 �m multimode fibre | 412 m |
| 1000Base-CX | 802.3z | 1 Gbps | Twinax copper (HSSDC) | 25 m |
| 1000Base-T | 802.3ab | 1 Gbps | Cat5 UTP, 4 pairs | 100 m |
| 1000Base-SX | 802.3z | 1 Gbps | Multimode fibre, 850 nm | 220 m (62.5 �m) / 550 m (50 �m) |
| 1000Base-LX | 802.3z | 1 Gbps | Single-mode fibre, 1300 nm | 3 km up to 10 km |
| 1000Base-ZX | Cisco | 1 Gbps | Single-mode fibre | 70 km (43.5 miles) |
| 10GBase-T | 802.3an | 10 Gbps | UTP (book: Cat5e, 6 or 7) | 100 m (book) - see correction below |
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

10GBase-T cable limits. UPDATED The book says 10GBase-T runs on Cat5e, 6 or 7 and supports the full 100 m, and elsewhere says Cat6 is "rated for 10 Gbps". In practice (Intel's X540 cable guide): Cat6a = 100 m, Cat6 = 55 m, Cat5e = not supported for 10GBASE-T. A cabling vendor summarising TIA TSB-155-A adds that 10GBASE-T can operate over up to 37 m of installed Cat6, and between 37 and 55 m depending on crosstalk from neighbouring cables. So use Cat6a for new 10 Gbps copper runs.
What stays true: Cat5e is fine for 1000Base-T (Gigabit) at 100 m, as the book says.
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)

Shared media versus point-to-point (v1.1 objective 1.3). ADDED Shared media means many devices share one wire or one hub, so they share one collision domain and must take turns (the old CSMA/CD method). Examples: coax bus, hubs. Point-to-point means a link between exactly two devices, like a switch port to a PC, a switch-to-switch link or a router-to-router WAN link. Modern switched Ethernet is point-to-point and normally runs full-duplex, so collisions should not happen on it. If you see collisions on a switched link, suspect a duplex mismatch (see the troubleshooting guide in this document).
Quick check 1.4
Q10. You must run 10 Gbps over copper for 90 metres in a new building. Which cable do you choose?
A. Cat5e
B. Cat6
C. Cat6a
D. Cat3
Answer: C - Cat6a supports 10GBASE-T to 100 m. Cat6 only reaches about 55 m, and Cat5e is not supported.
Q11. What do we call signal loss as it travels along a cable?
Answer: Attenuation - crosstalk is interference between pairs, which is a different problem.
BOOK The most common cable today is Category 5e UTP (up to a gigabit at up to 100 m). The book says to know three cable types: straight-through, crossover and rolled.
1.5.1 Straight-Through Cable, book p. 20

Used between different kinds of device: host to switch (or hub) and router to switch (or hub). For 10/100 Mbps, only pins 1, 2, 3 and 6 are used: connect 11, 22, 33 and 66. One side transmits on pins 1 and 2 and the other side receives on them, and the pair on pins 3 and 6 works the other way.
1.5.2 Crossover Cable, book pp. 20-22

Used between similar kinds of device: switch to switch, hub to hub, host to host, hub to switch, router direct to host, router to router. The same four wires are used, but crossed: pin 1  pin 3 and pin 2  pin 6 on each side.
Cable cheat sheet
| Connection | Cable (textbook rule) | Why |
| PC  Switch | Straight-through | PC and router transmit on 1,2. Switch and hub transmit on 3,6. Different = straight. |
| Router  Switch | Straight-through | Different types |
| Switch  Switch | Crossover | Same type |
| Router  Router | Crossover | Same type |
| PC  PC | Crossover | Same type |
| Router  PC | Crossover | Same type |
| Switch  Hub | Crossover | Both transmit on 3,6 |
MEMORY TIP
Memory tip: unlike devices  straight. Like devices  crossover. (Treat PC and router as one kind, and switch and hub as the other kind.)
Gigabit wiring (1000Base-T), book pp. 21-22

Gigabit copper uses all four pairs (all 8 pins) and every pair sends and receives at the same time. Straight-through is still 11 up to 88. A gigabit crossover crosses 13 and 26 and also 47 and 58.
WARNING
A 4-wire (pins 1, 2, 3, 6) cable only works for 10/100 Ethernet. The book warns it will not work for gigabit or voice.
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

Auto-MDIX. UPDATED The book notes that a straight-through cable between two switches may still work because of auto-MDIX (the port detects the cable and swaps its transmit and receive pairs). Intel's adapter documentation shows the same idea (automatic MDI/MDI-X) on modern NICs. In real life you will rarely need a crossover cable. For the exam, the book warns that the objectives do not normally treat auto-detect as valid, so answer with the textbook rule unless the question mentions auto-MDIX.
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)

Rolled (rollover) cable. ADDED CHECK The book says you must know three cable types, but this chapter does not explain the third one. A rolled cable (also called a console or rollover cable) connects your PC to the console port of a router or switch for management. Its wires are reversed end to end (pin 1 to pin 8, 2 to 7, and so on). Many newer devices also have a USB console port. I wrote this from general knowledge. Check your own device's console cable type.
1.5.3 Fibre Optic, book p. 22

BOOK Fibre carries light through glass (or plastic). It is very fast, very thin, can go very long distances and, unlike UTP, is immune to crosstalk and similar interference. It has three parts: the core (carries the light), the cladding (keeps the light inside the core) and the buffer (protects the glass). The standard cladding is 125 microns. A single-mode core is about 9 microns, thin compared with a human hair at about 50 microns.
|  | Single-mode (SMF) | Multimode (MMF) |
| Core size | Very small (about 9 �m) | Larger (50 or 62.5 �m) |
| Light paths | One mode of light | Many light paths that must be put back together at the receiver |
| Distance | Much farther (km to tens of km) | Shorter (hundreds of metres) |
| Cost | More expensive | Cheaper |
| Book examples | 1000Base-LX, 1000Base-ZX | 100Base-FX, 1000Base-SX |
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)

Connectors and modules. ADDED The book says there are about 70 fibre connectors and Cisco uses a few. The ones you will meet most are SC, ST and LC. Switches usually take fibre through pluggable SFP/SFP+ transceiver modules, which must match the fibre type (single-mode or multimode) and the other end. A common real fault is mixing single-mode and multimode, or swapping the transmit and receive fibres.
1.5.4 Power over Ethernet (802.3af, 802.3at), book pp. 23-24

BOOK PoE sends electrical power and data together over normal twisted-pair cable, so you can power IP phones, wireless access points, cameras and small switches without a nearby wall socket. The device that supplies power is the PSE; the device that receives it is the PD. Power comes either from a PoE-capable switch port or from a power injector. Never use both at once, and make sure an injector gives the right voltage for the device.
| Standard | Name | Type | Max power at the switch (PSE) | Power available at the device (PD) |
| IEEE 802.3af | PoE | Type 1 | 15.4 W | 12.95 W |
| IEEE 802.3at | PoE+ | Type 2 | 30 W | 25.5 W |
| IEEE 802.3bt | PoE++ (4-pair) | Type 3 | 60 W | 51 W |
| IEEE 802.3bt | PoE++ (4-pair) | Type 4 | 90 W | about 71 W |
Figures from vendor summaries of the IEEE standards (TP-Link, Microchip and Nexans documents all agree on these values). The PD figure is lower because some power is lost in the cable.
UPDATED / MODERN NOTE

802.3bt is missing from the book. UPDATED The book only covers 802.3af and 802.3at, and one sentence about 802.3at is garbled. The correct, simple version: 802.3af = 15.4 W, 802.3at (PoE+) = 30 W. Newer 802.3bt raises this to 60 W and 90 W by using all four pairs. Planning a switch? Add up the maximum power for every powered device and compare it with the switch's total PoE budget.
Command breakdown: PoE on a Catalyst switch
Common IOS PoE commands CHECK (needs a PoE-capable switch; not all simulators support them)
Switch# show power inline
Switch(config)# interface gigabitEthernet 1/0/5
Switch(config-if)# power inline auto
- show power inline lists each port, whether it is supplying power, and how much.
- power inline auto (usually the default) lets the switch detect a powered device and supply power.
- power inline never turns PoE off on that port.
CHECK I could not run these commands on a real switch in this session. Check the exact options with power inline ? on your device.
EXAM CRITICAL

v2.0 lists PoE under configuring edge-host switch ports (phones, access points). Know the standards (af, at, bt), the PSE/PD words, and the fact that an injector and a switch port are two alternatives.
Quick check 1.5
Q12. Which pins are crossed to make a 10/100 crossover cable?
D. 36 only
Answer: B - pin 1 goes to pin 3 and pin 2 goes to pin 6. For gigabit you also cross 47 and 58.
Q13. Which IEEE standard is called PoE+ and how much power can the switch port supply?
Answer: 802.3at, 30 W - 802.3af gives 15.4 W and 802.3bt gives 60 W or 90 W.
Q14. Why can a 4-wire straight-through cable (pins 1, 2, 3, 6) be a problem on a gigabit link?
Answer: Gigabit uses all four pairs (8 wires) - a 4-wire cable only works for 10/100.
ADDED (NOT IN THE BOOK)

ADDED The book does this in Chapter 18, but both v1.1 (objective 1.4) and v2.0 (objective 1.1, "diagnose interface and cable issues") test it, and it uses the cables from this chapter. Here is the start of the skill.
Read the interface status first
| show ip interface brief shows | Meaning | First thing to check |
| down / down | Layer 1 problem. No link. | Cable unplugged or broken, wrong cable, other end powered off or shut down, wrong fibre type |
| administratively down / down | Someone typed shutdown. | no shutdown on the interface |
| up / down | Link detected but Layer 2 not working | Encapsulation or clocking (serial), speed/duplex mismatch, other end problem |
| up / up | Layers 1 and 2 are working | If traffic still fails, check IP addressing, VLANs and routing |
Command breakdown: show interfaces
Illustrative output (your counters will differ)
Switch# show interfaces fastEthernet 0/1
FastEthernet0/1 is up, line protocol is up (connected)
Full-duplex, 100Mb/s
12 input errors, 12 CRC, 0 frame, 0 overrun, 0 ignored
0 output errors, 0 collisions, 0 interface resets
0 late collision, 0 deferred
- is up, line protocol is up: first word = Layer 1, second = Layer 2.
- Full-duplex, 100Mb/s: what the link actually negotiated. Compare it with the other end.
- input errors / CRC: damaged frames arriving. Often a bad cable, a bad connector, interference or a duplex mismatch.
- collisions / late collision: should be zero on a switched full-duplex link. Late collisions are a classic sign of a duplex mismatch or a cable that is too long.
Symptom guide
| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
| Link down, no lights | Bad or wrong cable, unplugged, far end off | Reseat, swap the cable, check the other end and shutdown state |
| Link up but very slow, errors and late collisions | Duplex mismatch (one side full, one half) | Set both ends to auto, or both to the same fixed speed and duplex |
| Link down after setting a fixed speed on one side only | Speed mismatch | Match the speed on both ends, or use auto on both |

| CRC errors rising on a copper link | Damaged cable or connector, interference, or a run that is too long (over 100 m) | Replace the cable, re-terminate, shorten the run, move away from power cables |
| Link flaps (up and down repeatedly) | Loose or damaged connector, failing cable or transceiver | Replace the cable and the transceiver and check the connectors |
| Fibre link down | Single-mode/multimode mismatch, transmit and receive swapped, dirty connector, wrong transceiver | Check the fibre type at both ends, swap the fibre pair, clean the connectors |

| PoE device does not power on | Port set to power inline never, switch PoE budget used up, or device needs more power than the port supplies | show power inline, check the budget and standard (af/at/bt) |
CHECK These symptoms are standard networking practice, but I did not test them on hardware in this session. Confirm each one in your lab in the Labs section.
| Topic | Remember |
| Switch vs router | Switch: Layer 2, reads frame MAC addresses. Router: Layer 3, reads IP addresses in packets and splits broadcast domains. |
| Domains | Hub: 1 collision + 1 broadcast. Switch: 1 collision per port, 1 broadcast. Router: splits broadcast domains. |
| Switch learning | Learn source, forward by destination, flood unknown and broadcast. |
| NGFW | Layer 7 inspection, AVC, IPS, URL filtering, TLS decryption, NAT, VPN, QoS, REST API. Cisco: Secure Firewall Threat Defense (formerly Firepower). |
| 3-tier | Core = fast and reliable, no ACLs. Distribution = policy, routing, filtering. Access = connect users, microsegmentation. Layers are logical. |
| 2-tier (collapsed core) | Core and distribution merged. Cheaper, for smaller campuses. |
| Spine-leaf | Data centre. Leaf = ToR switch. Every leaf connects to every spine. Spines connect only to leaves. One spine hop between leaves. |
| WAN terms | CPE, CSU/DSU (clocking), demarc, local loop, CO (POP), toll network. |
| Cables | Straight: host-switch, router-switch (pins 1,2,3,6). Crossover: like devices (13, 26). Gigabit uses all 8 pins; gigabit crossover also 47, 58. |
| Fibre | Single-mode: tiny core, long distance, costs more. Multimode: larger core, shorter distance. Immune to crosstalk. |
| PoE | af 15.4 W; at (PoE+) 30 W; bt 60/90 W. PSE gives, PD receives. Switch port or injector, never both. |
| 10 Gbps copper | Cat6a 100 m; Cat6 about 55 m; Cat5e not supported. |
| Interface status | down/down = Layer 1; up/down = Layer 2; administratively down = shutdown. |

Status choices: Not assessed � Know � Partially understand � Need to learn � Needs revision. Rule: use Know only if you answered correctly without help or finished the lab without the answer in front of you.
- Core (move traffic fast and reliably, no ACLs or filtering), Distribution (routing, filtering, policy, WAN access), Access (connect users and devices, separate collision domains).

- Hub: one collision domain, one broadcast domain. Switch: one collision domain per port, one broadcast domain (by default). Router: one collision domain per interface and one broadcast domain per interface (it separates broadcast domains).

- A crossover cable. Pin 1 connects to pin 3 and pin 2 connects to pin 6 (gigabit also crosses 47 and 58). Many modern ports use auto-MDIX and will work with straight-through, but the textbook answer is crossover.

- Single-mode has a very small core (about 9 �m), carries one mode of light and goes much farther (and costs more). Multimode has a larger core (50 or 62.5 �m), carries many light paths and goes shorter distances. Single-mode goes farther.
- PoE sends power and data over the same Ethernet cable. 802.3at is PoE+ (30 W at the port).

sections.title: How far this has been tested

content.text: Nothing in this document was run on real Cisco hardware. Commands, sample outputs and lab results are written from standard IOS usage. Test them in your lab and correct anything that differs on your platform.
WARNING

Before you start. I cannot run a Cisco simulator for you. These labs are written for Cisco Packet Tracer (or GNS3/CML for the commands). After each lab, record your real result in the tracker row (the Practical lab column and Evidence / mistakes). Simulator behaviour for cables, PoE and error counters differs from real hardware, so write down what you actually saw.
Topology: Switch S1 has five ports: P1PC1, P2PC2, P3PC3, P4Hub H1 (H1 has PC4 and PC5 attached), P5Router R1 (G0/0). Switch S2 has three ports: P1PC6, P2PC7, P3Router R1 (G0/1).
Task: count the collision domains and the broadcast domains. Write your answer before reading on.
**What the book says**

Solution. Collision domains = 8. On S1: P1, P2, P3 (3) + P4 together with H1, PC4 and PC5 (1) + the S1-R1 link (1) = 5. On S2: P1, P2 (2) + the S2-R1 link (1) = 3. Broadcast domains = 2: everything on the S1 side including R1 G0/0, and everything on the S2 side including R1 G0/1.

labs.title: Watch a switch learn (Packet Tracer, 15 minutes)

content.text: - Place one 2960 switch and three PCs. Connect each PC to the switch with a straight-through cable.
- On the switch, run show mac address-table before any traffic. Write down what you see.
- From PC1, run ping 192.168.1.2 (the first ping may drop while ARP resolves).
- On the switch, run show mac address-table again.

Expected result: after step 5 you should see dynamic entries for the MAC addresses of the PCs that sent frames, each on the port it is connected to. PC3 may not appear yet because it has not sent anything. Why: the switch learns from source addresses only.
Challenge: ping PC3 from PC1 and run the command again. What changed? What does that tell you about the learning rule?
- Build: PC1 - Switch S1 - Switch S2 - PC2, plus Router R1 connected to S1.
- Use the cheat sheet in section 1.5 to choose each cable. Connect them.
- Now replace the S1-S2 cable with the wrong type for the textbook rule. Record the link light colour and whether the link comes up.
- Repeat with a PC-to-switch link using a crossover cable.

What to learn: the textbook rule says some pairs need crossover. Your simulator may bring the link up anyway because of auto-MDIX. Write down which of your attempts worked and which did not. That is real evidence about the difference between the exam rule and device behaviour. CHECK Behaviour differs between device models in the simulator.
Commands for Lab 1.4
Switch> enable
Switch# show ip interface brief
Switch# show interfaces fastEthernet 0/1
Switch# configure terminal
Switch(config)# interface fastEthernet 0/1
Switch(config-if)# speed 10
Switch(config-if)# duplex half
Switch(config-if)# end
Switch# show interfaces fastEthernet 0/1
- Record the status, speed and duplex of Fa0/1 before the change.
- Apply the commands above to one side of a link only.
- Record what happens to the link and to the line protocol.
- Undo the change with speed auto, duplex auto (or no speed, no duplex) and confirm the link recovers.

Expected result: forcing a different speed on one side only will usually take the link down or make the two ends disagree. A pure duplex mismatch usually keeps the link up but real equipment will show errors and late collisions. CHECK The simulator may not show collision counters realistically, so describe what you really see.

A 24-port switch has a 370 W PoE budget. You plan to connect 10 access points that each need a full 802.3at (30 W) allocation and 8 IP phones that each need a full 802.3af (15.4 W) allocation. Is the budget enough?
**What the book says**

Solution. APs: 10 x 30 W = 300 W. Phones: 8 x 15.4 W = 123.2 W. Total = 423.2 W. That is 53.2 W more than 370 W, so the budget is not enough on a worst-case basis. Real devices often draw less than their maximum, but you plan with the worst case. The budget number (370 W) is made up for the exercise; real switch budgets are in the product datasheet.

content.text: Q1 A switch receives a frame whose destination MAC address is not in its MAC address table. What does it do?
A. Drops it
B. Sends it back out of the port it arrived on
C. Floods it out of all other ports
D. Sends it to the router
Answer: C - unknown unicast frames are flooded out of every port except the incoming one.
Q2 Eight PCs connect to one switch (one PC per port), and the switch connects to one router interface. How many broadcast domains exist?
Answer: One - a switch does not split broadcast domains. The router interface is in the same one.
Q3 Name the two ways a router helps reduce traffic problems on a LAN.
Answer: It does not forward broadcasts by default, and it can filter by Layer 3 information. - these are the two advantages the book gives.
Q4 Which feature lets an NGFW allow a company app but block a game running on the same port?
A. NAT
B. Application Visibility and Control
C. VLAN trunking
D. Port security
Answer: B - AVC identifies the application, not only the port number.
Q5 In one sentence, what is the difference between an IDS and an IPS?
Answer: A - n IDS only alerts; an IPS sits in the traffic path and can block. - that is the whole idea behind "detection" versus "prevention".
Q6 Which layer of the 3-tier model should avoid access lists and packet filtering, and why?
A. Access
B. Distribution
C. Core
D. All of them
Answer: C - the core should switch traffic as fast as possible; policy belongs in the distribution layer.
Q7 In a spine-leaf design, what do spine switches connect to?
A. Servers
B. Leaf switches only
C. Other spine switches and servers
D. Firewalls only
Answer: B - spines connect only to leaves; every leaf connects to every spine.
Q8 Which WAN device provides clocking to a router's serial interface?
Answer: The CSU/DSU - the book says clocking is the most important thing to remember about it.
Q9 Where does the provider's responsibility end?
Answer: A - t the demarc (demarcation point) - after that, the cabling and equipment are the customer's.
Q10 You must run 10 Gbps over copper for 90 metres in a new building. Which cable do you choose?
A. Cat5e
B. Cat6
C. Cat6a
D. Cat3
Answer: C - Cat6a supports 10GBASE-T to 100 m. Cat6 only reaches about 55 m, and Cat5e is not supported.
Q11 What do we call signal loss as it travels along a cable?
Answer: A - ttenuation - crosstalk is interference between pairs, which is a different problem.
Q12 Which pins are crossed to make a 10/100 crossover cable?
D. 36 only
Answer: B - pin 1 goes to pin 3 and pin 2 goes to pin 6. For gigabit you also cross 47 and 58.
Q13 Which IEEE standard is called PoE+ and how much power can the switch port supply?
Answer: 802.3at, 30 W - 802.3af gives 15.4 W and 802.3bt gives 60 W or 90 W.
Q14 Why can a 4-wire straight-through cable (pins 1, 2, 3, 6) be a problem on a gigabit link?
Answer: Gigabit uses all four pairs (8 wires) - a 4-wire cable only works for 10/100.
Q15 A company has a small campus and wants to save money while keeping most hierarchy benefits. Which design fits?
A. Spine-leaf
B. Collapsed core (2-tier)
C. Full mesh WAN
D. Hub and spoke with hubs
Answer: B - a collapsed core merges the core and distribution layers into one set of switches.
Q16 Which statement about a Layer 2 switch is TRUE?
A. It creates one collision domain for all ports
B. It creates one broadcast domain per port
C. It builds its table from source MAC addresses
D. It forwards frames based on IP addresses
Answer: C - a switch learns from source MAC addresses. It makes one collision domain per port and does not split broadcast domains.
Q17 What does an NGFW inspect that a traditional port-based firewall does not?
Answer: A - pplication-layer (Layer 7) content, with application visibility and control and IPS. - that is what makes it "next-generation".
Q18 A T1 line is made of how many DS0 channels and what is its speed?
Answer: 24 DS0 channels, 1.544 Mbps - E1 is the European version with 30 channels and 2.048 Mbps.
Q19 Single-mode or multimode: which has the smaller core and goes farther?
Answer: Single-mode - the tighter core lets one mode of light travel much farther.
Q20 Which standard delivers up to 15.4 W at the port?
C. 802.3bt Type 3
D. 802.3bt Type 4
Answer: B - 802.3af (PoE) gives 15.4 W at the PSE.
Q21 An interface shows "up / down". Is this a Layer 1 or Layer 2 problem?
Answer: Layer 2 - "up" means a link signal is detected (Layer 1 is fine); "down" protocol means Layer 2 is not working.
Q22 Name one cause of late collisions on a switched link.
Answer: A - duplex mismatch (or a cable that is too long) - late collisions should not happen on a healthy full-duplex switched link.
